Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 72, verse 18–28:

Allah's words: ﴿And the mosques are for Allah﴾. There are four opinions concerning it.

The first: they are the mosques which are the houses of prayer. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. Qatadah said: when the Jews and Christians entered their synagogues and churches, they committed shirk, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded the Muslims to be sincere to Him when they entered their mosques.

The second: the body parts upon which the servant prostrates. This is the view of Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Ibn al-Anbari, and al-Farra' mentioned it. The meaning then is: do not prostrate upon them to other than Him.

The third: the word "mosques" here refers to all the places on earth. This is the view of al-Hasan. The meaning then is: the whole earth is a place for prostration, so do not prostrate upon it to other than its Creator.

The fourth: "mosques" means the acts of prostration (sujud), for it is the plural of masjid. It is said: "sajadtu sujudan wa masjidan," just as it is said: "darabtu fi al-ardi darban wa madriban," and then it is pluralized, so it is said: "al-masajid" and "al-madarib." Ibn Qutaybah said: according to this, its singular would be "masjadan" with a fatha on the jim. The meaning: be sincere to Him, and do not prostrate to other than Him.

Then he returned to mention the jinn, and said, Exalted is He: ﴿And when the servant of Allah stood up﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿calling upon Him﴾, i.e., worshipping Him. He used to pray in the valley of Nakhlah, as its explanation has already preceded in [al-Ahqaf: 29]. ﴿They almost became about him a compacted mass﴾. Most readers recited "libadan" with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the ba'. Hisham on the authority of Ibn ʿAmir, and Ibn Muhaysin, recited "lubadan" with a damma on the lam and a fatha on the ba' with its lightening. Al-Farra' said: the meanings of the two readings are one. It is said: "libadah" and "lubadah." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that some of them would ride upon others. From this derives the word "libd," which is spread out as a carpet; and everything you attach to something, you have "labbadtahu" (made it adhere). A group, including al-Hasan and al-Jahdari, recited "lubban" with a damma on the lam and a shadda on the ba'. Al-Farra' said: according to this reading, it is an attribute of the men, like your saying "ruka'an" and "ruku'an," and "sujjadan" and "sujudan." Al-Zajjaj said: it is the plural of "labid," like "raki'" and "rukka'." There are three opinions concerning the meaning of the verse.

The first: it is Allah's report about the jinn, relating their condition. The meaning: when he stood up to pray, the jinn almost rode upon one another because of their crowding upon him, out of eagerness to hear the Qur'an. This was narrated by ʿAtiyyah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is the statement of the jinn to their people when they returned to them, describing to them the obedience of the companions of Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and their following him in bowing and prostration. So it is as if they said: when he stood up to pray, his companions almost became about him a compacted mass. This meaning is in the narration of Ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: the meaning is that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up with the call, the humans and jinn massed together and backed one another against him, to nullify the truth he had brought. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

Allah's words: ﴿Say: Indeed I only call upon my Lord﴾. ʿAsim and Hamzah recited "Qul innama adʿu rabbi" without an alif. The rest recited "Qala," as a report about the Prophet (ﷺ). Muqatil said: the disbelievers of Makkah said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "You have come with a great matter, the like of which has not been heard; turn back from it." So this verse was revealed.

Allah's words: ﴿Say: Indeed I do not possess for you any harm﴾, i.e., I do not repel it from you, ﴿nor any right guidance﴾, i.e., good; meaning Allah, Exalted, possesses that, not I. ﴿Say: No one will protect me from Allah, and I will not find any refuge other than Him﴾, i.e., if I disobey Him, no one will prevent Him from me. This is because they said: "Leave what you call to, and we will protect you." ﴿And I will not find any refuge other than Him﴾ — we have explained it in [al-Kahf: 27]. ﴿Except a notification from Allah﴾. In it are two aspects, which al-Farra' mentioned.

One of them: it is an exception from Allah's words ﴿I do not possess for you any harm or right guidance﴾, except that I convey to you.

The second: "No one will protect me from Allah if I do not convey His message." Ibn al-Sa'ib said the first, and Muqatil said the second. The first: that Muhammad (ﷺ) may know that Jibril has conveyed to him. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

The second: that Muhammad (ﷺ) may know that the messengers before him "had conveyed the messages of their Lord," and that Allah had preserved them and warded off from them. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: that the deniers of the messengers may know that the messengers had conveyed the messages of their Lord. This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may know that this exists manifestly, by which reward is due, as in His words: ﴿And Allah does not yet know those of you who strove﴾ [Al 'Imran: 142]. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The fifth: that the Prophet may know that the messengers before him had come to him and did not reach anyone else. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

Ruways, from Yaʿqub, recited "liyuʿlama" with a damma on the ya', in the passive form. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is also recited "litaʿlama" with a ta', meaning: that the jinn may know that the messengers had conveyed from their gods, by what they hoped for from eavesdropping. ﴿And He encompasses what is with them﴾, i.e., Allah knows what is with the messengers, ﴿and He has counted everything in number﴾, so nothing escapes Him, not even the atom or the mustard seed.
